parts.note: Arsenal is a London football club, and the pause between the two halves of its match is the break meant

explanation.surface: An exclamation of delight at a lucky chance for a football club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Break' reads as a stroke of luck, but it is the interval in a football match; Arsenal is a famous London football club.
explanation.definitionFit: The interval between the two periods of a football match is the players' rest break.

clue.text: Neck style that brings us to a standstill

definitions.text: that brings us to a standstill

explanation.surface: A fashion for the neck so striking it stops us in our tracks.
explanation.walkthrough: A halter neck is a style of top or dress tied behind the neck; read as 'halt-er', it is something that halts.
explanation.definitionFit: A dress style with a strap round the back of the neck, and something that makes us halt.

clue.text: Its rate being a penny for the old hack

definitions.text: Its rate being a penny for the old hack

parts.words: Its rate being a penny for the old hack
parts.note: a hack journalist was once paid by the line written, at a penny a line

explanation.surface: Something whose price is a single penny for a worn-out horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hack' suggests a horse, but it is a jobbing journalist, paid in the old days a penny a line.
explanation.definitionFit: Payment by the number of lines written, or the number of lines in a piece of print.

clue.text: Inaccuracy permitted to give clear tone

indicators.note: the letters of the words clear tone yield, or give, a new arrangement

explanation.surface: An instrument maker is allowed some error so long as the note is clear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to give' signals that CLEAR TONE is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: In engineering, the allowable margin of error in a measurement or part.

clue.text: Where winner and loser really change places

definitions.text: Where winner and loser really change places

parts.words: Where winner and loser really change places
parts.note: the side that lost the contest is the one that comes out ahead in principle or conscience

explanation.surface: A description of a contest whose result is turned upside down.
explanation.walkthrough: The defeated party claims to have won on principle, so the real winner is the loser.
explanation.definitionFit: A defeat that nevertheless shows the loser to be right or admirable in principle.

clue.text: Medicine Macbeth would have thrown to the dogs

definitions.text: Macbeth would have thrown to the dogs

explanation.surface: A remedy so useless a tragic Scottish king would toss it to the hounds.
explanation.walkthrough: In Shakespeare's play Macbeth says 'Throw physic to the dogs, I'll none of it.'
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for a remedy or drug, and the very thing Macbeth tells the doctor to fling to the dogs.

indicators.note: infinite means without an end, so the final letter of the clue's word for paradise is dropped

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: Someone sighs that heaven goes on for ever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'infinite' is read as 'without end', removing the final N; the 's is 'is', a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To breathe out heavily, as in the phrase to heave a sigh.

clue.text: Definite conditions of former tax limitations ?

explanation.surface: Rules laid down for limits on taxation in earlier times.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading takes 'set' as past (fixed earlier) and 'terms' as limits laid on a tax.
explanation.definitionFit: Fixed stipulations agreed in advance, and limits that were laid down in the past.

clue.text: Grants one put 'in for cypresses, for example

indicators.note: the numeral is put inside the word for granting, a container instruction

parts.note: to grant something is to confer it
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Funds awarded for planting evergreen trees such as cypresses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put in' places I inside CONFERS; the stray mark is from the printing.
explanation.definitionFit: Cypresses are cone-bearing evergreen trees, one example of the group.

explanation.surface: A note of correspondence addressed to the innkeeper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter' reads as a written message, but here it is one who lets property; 'mine host' is the old phrase for a pub or inn keeper.
explanation.definitionFit: One who lets out property, and the keeper of an inn, both known by this title.

clue.text: Market in type of bird for the house

definitions.text: type of bird for the house

parts.note: a mart is a market
taken as written

explanation.surface: A trader lists a market where pet birds are sold for the home.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the full bird name: the house martin nests under house eaves.
explanation.definitionFit: The house martin is a small swallow-like bird that builds its nest on buildings.

explanation.surface: A splendid dawn suits a climbing plant.
explanation.walkthrough: Ipomoea is the botanical name for the climbing plant whose trumpet flowers open in the morning.
explanation.definitionFit: A glorious dawn spectacle, and the climbing plant genus whose flowers open at daybreak.

clue.text: " It is a nipping and an air " (Hamlet)

definitions.text: " It is a nipping and an air " (Hamlet)

parts.words: " It is a nipping and an air " (Hamlet)
parts.note: a quotation from Shakespeare with one word blanked out, the missing adjective describing the cold night air on the battlements

explanation.surface: A line from Hamlet, complaining of the bitter night air, with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet, on the battlements waiting for the ghost, says 'It is a nipping and an eager air'; the missing word is the answer, in an old sense of keen or sharp.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's usage the word means sharp or biting, describing cold air.

parts.note: in autumn the leaves come loose from the trees, and a notebook with detachable pages is described the same way

explanation.surface: A diary kept during the autumn season.
explanation.walkthrough: A notebook whose pages can be taken out is described by the same phrase as a leaf falling from a tree in autumn.
explanation.definitionFit: A binder with removable pages is described by this term, and fallen autumn foliage is literally detached.

clue.text: Fine spell comes late for American red adder

explanation.surface: A fine spell of weather arrives late for an American snake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Adder' reads as the snake, but it is one who adds, a summer; 'American red' is the old term for a Native American, an Indian.
explanation.definitionFit: A warm sunny period in late autumn, and, read in two parts, an American Indian who adds up figures.

clue.text: Gives Neaera's hair a combing, for instance

definitions.text: Gives Neaera's hair a combing, for instance

parts.words: Gives Neaera's hair a combing, for instance
parts.note: Milton's Lycidas speaks of 'the tangles of Neaera's hair', so combing them out removes the knots

explanation.surface: Someone grooming a classical maiden's locks.
explanation.walkthrough: Milton's poem Lycidas mentions sporting 'with the tangles of Neaera's hair'; combing them out is an example of the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Combing hair straightens out the knots, one example of freeing what is snarled.

parts.note: 'inferior' is used in its literal sense of lower, a force pushing from below that lifts an object in a fluid

explanation.surface: A remark on how a weaker army can still achieve something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inferior force' suggests a weaker army, but means a force acting from beneath, as buoyancy does in physics.
explanation.definitionFit: The buoyant pressure a fluid exerts upwards on a body immersed in it.

parts.note: after confessing sins, the priest sets acts of self-mortification as atonement

explanation.surface: The embarrassing fallout of owning up to something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mortifying' reads as embarrassing, but means mortifying the flesh, the acts of atonement set after a confession to a priest.
explanation.definitionFit: Acts of atonement imposed by a priest after sins have been confessed.

parts.note: 'your lot' is your fate or destiny, so to decide it beforehand is to fix fate in advance

explanation.surface: Someone announcing that no more will be handed out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's your lot' sounds like 'no more for you', but 'lot' is fate, and deciding fate beforehand is the theological sense of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: To ordain in advance, as divine will is said to fix a person's destiny.

parts.note: a bit of something is a piece of it

explanation.surface: A small portion handed out to everybody.
explanation.definitionFit: Means for every one individually, as in costing a pound per item.

parts.note: close means near
a T-junction is shaped like the letter T

explanation.surface: A secluded room located close to a road junction.
explanation.definitionFit: A small private chamber or cupboard for storage or retreat.

clue.text: Before a fire it gives basic cover

definitions.text: Before a fire it gives basic cover

parts.words: Before a fire it gives basic cover
parts.note: a mat lying in front of the fireplace covers the base of the floor there

explanation.surface: A description of something giving rudimentary protection ahead of a blaze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Basic cover' sounds like minimal insurance, but it means a covering on the floor (the base) in front of the fireplace.
explanation.definitionFit: A mat placed on the floor in front of a fireplace.

parts.note: the proverb says once bitten, the victim is then shy a second time

explanation.surface: Someone who became timid after a dog bit them.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'once bitten, twice shy' supplies the missing word.
explanation.definitionFit: Means on two occasions, the second half of the proverb about caution after being hurt.

indicators.note: a crash wrecks things, so the letters of the word plane are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: An aircraft goes down somewhere in a country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crash' rearranges PLANE into the Himalayan country.
explanation.definitionFit: A Himalayan kingdom, now a republic, between India and China.

explanation.surface: A spiny animal discovered on the road.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is an old name for the hedgehog, and a 'street' one is a ragged child living on the streets.
explanation.definitionFit: An old name for the spiny mammal, and a scruffy child, as in the phrase street urchin.

parts.note: hydroponics is growing plants in water with no earth, which is why it involves no dirt

explanation.surface: An enthusiast praises the tidiness of growing plants in water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clean' suggests spotless, but the point is that hydroponics uses no soil at all, so it is literally dirt-free.
explanation.definitionFit: Hydroponic growing is done entirely without earth, in nutrient-rich water.

explanation.surface: A query about whether some man inspects the bedspread.
explanation.walkthrough: A tester is someone who examines, and also the canopy over a four-poster bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who examines or checks things, and a canopy hung over a bed.

parts.note: eyes are the organs that see, so they are seers
someone who departed has left

explanation.surface: Prophets have gone away from a military religious order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seers' looks like prophets, but means the organs of sight; 'military order' is a parade-ground command, not a body like the Templars.
explanation.definitionFit: A command on parade telling soldiers to turn their heads to the side.
